assessment.success_condition: Observed overall conversion in the treatment arm exceeds 22.22% (an absolute lift of +3.22 percentage points), generating contribution per customer above Rs.39.33.
assessment.failure_condition: Observed treatment conversion remains at or below 22.21%, resulting in net contribution per customer falling below the Rs.39.33 baseline.
assessment.selection_rationale: Baseline contribution per customer is Rs.39.33 (19.0% * Rs.207). Break-even conversion thresholds: 1) int_shipping (Rs.30 cost, Rs.177 contribution/order): 22.22% (+3.22% lift required); 2) int_bundle (Rs.43.10 cost assuming Rs.85 basket add, Rs.186.19 contribution/order): 21.12% (+2.12% lift required, contingent on basket expansion); 3) int_pct (Rs.38.85 cost, Rs.168.15 contribution/order): 23.39% (+4.39% lift required); 4) int_flat (Rs.60 cost, Rs.147 contribution/order): 26.75% (+7.75% lift required). int_shipping is the most affordable direct price-cut intervention. int_shipping provides the lowest friction barrier for the 40% cart abandoner segment with a modest break-even threshold of +3.22% conversion lift. While int_bundle mathematically requires a lower lift (+2.12%), it relies on an unverified assumption of basket expansion across customers who historically buy small single items.

assessment.reasoning: With contribution margins already squeezed by recent freight rate increases, running an unsegmented promotional experiment during a quiet season will erode contribution. Cart abandoners represent only 9% of customers, so any blanket intervention (like free shipping or flat discounts) subsidizes the 91% of buyers who would convert anyway, including price-insensitive bulk regulars (14%). The single allowed experiment costs roughly 2.8x the annual promotional profit pool, making the risk of margin destruction far outweigh any potential gain.

assessment.best_option_considered: int_shipping (Free shipping, waiving Rs.30 per order). To break even, baseline conversion must rise from 15.60% to 16.59% (an absolute lift of +0.99 percentage points) to offset the Rs.30 cost per converted order.
assessment.expected_value_reasoning: Baseline contribution per visit is Rs.78.47 (15.6% * Rs.503). Waiving Rs.30 shipping reduces contribution per order to Rs.473, requiring conversion to reach 16.59% (+0.99% absolute lift) to break even. Because shipping sensitivity is limited to the 9% cart abandoner segment, even a massive conversion boost within that sub-group would not generate the aggregate site-wide lift required to cover the Rs.30 subsidy paid across all 100% of converting traffic. Given the high fixed cost of running our single experiment relative to potential upside, the expected value of running any intervention is negative.

assessment.success_condition: Conversion rate among treated customers reaches or exceeds 18.5% with average order value increasing toward Rs.2,541, yielding net contribution per customer above the baseline Rs.125.15.

assessment.selection_rationale: Baseline contribution per customer is Rs.125.15 (15.3% conversion * Rs.818 margin). 1) int_shipping (Rs.80 cost): Net margin Rs.738/order, requires 16.96% conversion (+1.66% absolute lift). 2) int_bundle: Basket increases to Rs.2,541, pre-discount margin Rs.958, less 11% discount (Rs.279.51) = Net margin Rs.678.49/order, requires 18.45% conversion (+3.15% absolute lift). 3) int_flat (Rs.140 discount): Net margin Rs.678/order, requires 18.46% conversion (+3.16% absolute lift). 4) int_pct (10% discount = Rs.216.90): Net margin Rs.601.10/order, requires 20.82% conversion (+5.52% absolute lift). Although int_shipping has a lower required conversion lift (+1.66%), int_bundle (+3.15% required lift) is uniquely backed by explicit customer service feedback requesting bundles of co-bought SKUs. By increasing basket value by Rs.372, int_bundle expands customer order size rather than merely discounting existing single-item orders, making it the most structurally sound intervention to generate positive incremental contribution.

Running any promotional experiment right now risks heavily subsidizing baseline demand (27% bulk regulars who are price-insensitive) and margin-eroding deal seekers (41%), while consuming the merchant's single remaining experiment attempt (costing ~2.8x annual promo profit pool) to solve problems that discounts cannot fix.

assessment.best_option_considered: int_bundle (Bundle offer at 6% off adding ~Rs.167 basket value, pairing slow-moving Classic millet muesli with a high-velocity SKU).
assessment.expected_value_reasoning: Baseline contribution per order is Rs.635 (32% of Rs.1,983). A bundle increasing order value to Rs.2,150 with a 6% discount (Rs.129 off) yields a gross margin of Rs.688 minus Rs.129 discount = Rs.559 net contribution per order. To break even against the baseline order contribution of Rs.635 at 8.1% conversion, overall conversion would need to jump to at least 9.2% (+1.1% absolute lift, or a 13.6% relative increase) across all treated traffic. Because baseline buyers would adopt the bundle and yield lower per-order contribution (Rs.559 vs Rs.635), and given that one experiment costs 2.8x the annual promotional profit pool, the expected contribution gain does not clear the hurdle rate required for this single remaining test.

assessment.prediction: Waiving the Rs.50 shipping fee will eliminate the primary friction point for cart abandoners, raising conversion from 4.6% to at least 5.8% (a +1.2% absolute lift), exceeding the break-even threshold of 5.73%.
assessment.reasoning: The merchant's trading notes show conversion is drifting down despite rising sessions. Customer service themes and segment data explicitly pinpoint shipping costs as the dominant bottleneck at checkout—cart abandoners make up 28% of traffic and mention shipping fees more than product price, while customer support reports repeated inquiries about free shipping. Waiving the Rs.50 shipping fee directly addresses this validated drop-off reason. At a reduced contribution of Rs.203 per order, a conversion rate of 5.73% (+1.13% absolute lift) achieves break-even contribution.

For int_flat (Rs.70 off), new margin is Rs.183, requiring a 6.36% conversion (+1.76% absolute lift) to break even. For int_pct (9% off = Rs.75.24), new margin is Rs.177.76, requiring a 6.55% conversion (+1.95% absolute lift). Solving the direct cause of conversion drift provides the highest grounded probability of yielding net positive incremental contribution.

assessment.reasoning: Experimentation is scarce and expensive, costing roughly 2.8x the merchant's annual promotion profit pool. Nestwell Studio operates in a market where price elasticity is low—its nearest competitor raised prices by ~8% without losing share. Furthermore, 35% of the customer base consists of price-insensitive Gift buyers (25%) and Bulk regulars (10%) who buy on salary weeks or care strictly about delivery speed. Universal discounts or free shipping subsidize baseline sales from these segments. Free shipping (int_shipping) costs Rs. 160 per order, requiring conversion to rise from 5.6% to 6.87% (+1.27% absolute lift) just to break even on contribution; however, a previous trial already showed free shipping lifts conversion without guaranteeing net contribution profitability. Discounting or bundling co-bought items gives away margin on existing organic behavior. Declining to run an experiment preserves profit margin and avoids wasting the merchant's single experiment budget.
